contributions.headingText:
FNAB has a long history of providing accurate diagnoses in patients with both palpable and impalpable breast lesions. Breast FNAB provides a rapid, accurate, and cost-effective diagnosis, with the procedure being well accepted and tolerated by patients. FNAB is able, in the vast majority of cases, to distinguish benign from malignant breast lesions. Appropriate patient management is reliant on this distinction {32749785; 33755356; 34029451; 21660275}. The ROM for a benign breast lesion diagnosed on FNAB ranges from 1% to 3% [[Field AS, Raymond WA, Schmitt F, editors. The International Academy of Cytology Yokohama system for reporting breast fine needle aspiration biopsy cytopathology. 1st ed. Cham (Switzerland): Springer; 2020.]]. Depending on the specific benign lesion, management may include surgery or non-surgical options, such as treatment of infection or regular patient follow-up. Breast disease is broadly divided into benign and malignant with the majority being benign. Benign breast disease is 10 times more common in most settings than breast malignancy {30990294; 27866091; 35168773}. In several published series of breast FNABs, the majority of diagnoses are benign and account for between 24% and 77.5% of total cases {21660275; 33755356; 32749785; 34029451}.

Both infectious and non-infectious benign lesions can be diagnosed on FNAB. These include abscess, granulomatous mastitis, intramammary lymphadenopathy, fat necrosis, lactational change, gynaecomastia, foreign body reaction to agents such as silicone, fibroadenoma, and fibrocystic disease. In most breast FNAB series, fibroadenoma is the most common lesion seen. The second and third most common lesions are abscess / acute mastitis and cyst, respectively {34866246}. These commonly encountered entities are selected to be included in our discussion. Even if a lesion is benign, it may still be associated with significant morbidity such as breast abscess. FNAB allows for rapid management of breast abscess, albeit incision and drainage or antimicrobial agents. Likewise in cases of granulomatous inflammation, FNAB and microbiological investigations will determine if there is an infectious cause that can then be treated appropriately. FNAB of a cyst allows for both diagnosis and treatment in the form of cyst drainage. Even if a lesion appears benign clinically and on imaging, having a laboratory diagnosis can be very reassuring to patient and clinician alike {32749785; 33755356; 34029451; 21660275; 34866246} [[Nargund A, Mohan RH, Pai MM, et al. Demystifying breast FNACs based on the international academy of cytology yokohama breast cytopathology system: a retrospective study. J Clin Diagn Res. 2021;15(3):EC01–EC05. doi:10.7860/JCDR/2021/45366/14606.]].

A specific FNAB diagnosis is not possible in all benign breast lesions. Some lesions included in our discussion are uncommon and the cytomorphology may not be well described. Others included are involved in differential diagnosis from malignant lesions. The broad management of a lesion deemed benign on cytology is similar. Correlation with the clinical and imaging findings (triple test) is always advisable if possible. Apart from the aforementioned entities, other benign lesions include hamartoma, intraductal papilloma, radial scar / complex sclerosing lesion, benign phyllodes tumour, epithelial-myoepithelial tumour, spindle cell tumours, lipoma and angiolipoma, granular cell tumour, and tumours of the nipple. If the clinical and imaging findings are in keeping with a benign cytopathological diagnosis, then routine follow-up is required. The exception would be an infective process. If those features are not in keeping with the benign cytology, then other investigations are indicated [[Field AS, Raymond WA, Schmitt F, editors. The International Academy of Cytology Yokohama system for reporting breast fine needle aspiration biopsy cytopathology. 1st ed. Cham (Switzerland): Springer; 2020.]].

For some breast-specific entities, including non-invasive lobular neoplasia (atypical lobular hyperplasia, classic lobular carcinoma in situ, florid lobular carcinoma in situ), usual ductal hyperplasia, atypical ductal hyperplasia, and columnar cell lesions (including flat epithelial atypia, microglandular adenosis, lactating adenoma, and duct adenoma), specific cytopathological diagnoses cannot be make, as the accurate diagnosis of these requires assessment of the architecture and lesional size, and demonstration of an absence of myoepithelial cells, information which is not available in FNAB preparation, Thus, these entities are not included in this section.

Other mesenchymal lesions are also not covered in this section, including different forms of vascular tumours (haemangioma, perilobular haemangioma, venous haemangioma, cavernous haemangioma, capillary haemangioma, angiomatosis, atypical vascular lesion, lymphatic atypical vascular lesion resembling lymphangioma, and vascular atypical vascular lesion resembling haemangioma) and smooth muscle tumours (leiomyoma, cutaneous leiomyoma, and leiomyoma of the nipple and areola). The cytopathological features of these are similar to those of their counterparts in other organs systems and are not discussed in this section.
